stage: GENERATOR ONLY - candidate slate, no verdicts, no orders, no sizing. Court intake for the pipeline.
parent_record: desk/data/edge_classifications/AI_ADOPTER_20260802.json (large-cap version). The unresolved parent question - are savings RETAINED or competed away - is carried per name as retention_proxy.
thesis: Companies whose cost-to-serve is dominated by ops personnel (servicing, claims, back-office, underwriting ops, customer support) are quietly converting that cost to software; the opex ratio falls before consensus models it. Small/mid-cap paper, $300M-$10B.

method.universe: 80 live US names across insurance brokers/TPAs, title, BPO/CX, specialty and mortgage servicers, collections, staffing, claims/RCM processors, exchanges and market-data ops, and payroll/HCM.
method.ops_intensity: SG&A or total opex over revenue from the latest annual income statement (yfinance, screen-grade, marked per name) PLUS the audited personnel ratio where the issuer tags LaborAndRelatedExpense in XBRL - that tag is the real ops-intensity metric and it is the FAF-template signal.
method.margin_trend: 8 quarters of operating margin, SG&A/revenue and personnel/revenue recomputed from SEC XBRL companyconcept (data.sec.gov), NOT from yfinance - yfinance caps at 5 quarters. Q4 derived as FY minus the first three quarters.
method.ai_program_check: Primary-source pass over each company's latest 10-K, latest 10-Q and 2026 8-K EX-99.1 earnings releases, pulled from EDGAR Archives and grepped for AI/automation/headcount/efficiency language. Graded on venue (10-K/10-Q > 8-K > deck) and on whether a NUMBER is attached.
method.live_prices: IBKR snapshot pulled this run for every top-8 name before any range or percentile statement.
known_gaps: Earnings-call TRANSCRIPT tier was not reached - the session web-search budget was exhausted, so all findings are filed-document only. A CFO who quantified a saving verbally and never wrote it down reads here as 'NO NAMED PROGRAM'. Most material for CRVL, ECPG, MMS, EXLS, CNDT, TTEC.
PCTY FY2026 10-K was imminent at check time - re-pull owed.
OTCM is not an SEC registrant - UNVERIFIABLE, not clean.
5 names returned no usable XBRL series: GBLI, EXLS, NNI, VEL (tag mismatch) - these are coverage failures, not clean reads.

tag_selection_lesson: SEC XBRL tag choice must prefer the MOST RECENT series, not the first tag that returns >=6 facts. The legacy 'Revenues' tag is still populated for many issuers with data ending 2015-2019 and silently wins a naive first-match, producing a stale denominator against a current numerator (this produced nonsense ratios for PFSI, MMS, ONIT, OTCM on the first pass). Fixed by scoring candidate tags on (latest fact date, fact count).

counts.inflection_definition: operating margin last-4-quarter average at least +1.5pp above the prior-4-quarter average AND the SG&A or personnel ratio falling at least 0.3pp over the same 8 audited quarters - margin up WITH the cost ratio down, so revenue mix and cycle alone do not qualify
counts.of_those_inflecting_with_a_filed_QUANTIF: 3 firm (LMND, PAYC, ALIT) + 1 partial (MMS, technology-attributed not AI-attributed)
the_four: PAYC (headcount 7,306->5,770 = -21.0% on revenue +9.0%, 10-K) - VERIFIED EXACT this run
ALIT (>$75M annual savings, 10-K and 10-Q, AI named as one of four levers) - VERIFIED EXACT, AI share unquantified
MMS - DOWNGRADED on verification: the filing says 'technology initiatives', not AI, and it is one item in a five-driver list. Counts as a partial at best.
counts.names_with_NO_named_internal_AI_cost_pro: roughly 45 of the ~60 checked - where an AI proper noun exists it is almost always a PRODUCT sold to clients (EXLerate.ai, Code Harbor, Wave iX, Everforth Adapt, Kelly Helix, AltitudeAI, Clover Assistant, Unisys Intelligence Accelerator), not a cost-to-serve initiative
counts.inflection_count_is_a_lower_bound: The 18 count tested the SG&A and personnel ratios only. A targeted cost-of-revenue re-test on 26 previously-flat names found 11 more with falling cost ratios, HQY at -5.15pp among them. Treat 18 as a floor.

structural_findings: THE D2 CONJUNCTION IS AS EMPTY DOWN-CAP AS IT WAS UP-CAP. The large-cap pass found exactly one company tying AI to a quantified cost outcome in a filed document. Down-cap the count is four out of ~80. This replicates rather than refutes the parent finding.

PRICING BASIS IS THE REAL DISCRIMINANT, NOT SECTOR. Self-cannibalizing (per-FTE / per-hour / per-minute / per-seat): TTEC, IBEX, CRAI, MAN, RHI, FCN, KELYA, plus the T&M halves of ICFI, EFOR, UIS. Keepable (per-participant / transaction / outcome / subscription): ALIT, MMS, the contingency-fee slice of CNDT, KFY's Digital. A name in a 'good' sector with per-FTE pricing cannot keep the gain, and vice versa.

THE DISRUPTION LEG NOW HAS AN EMPIRICAL INSTANCE, NOT JUST A THEORY. Robert Half discloses Protiviti revenue flat at $1.95B because average hourly bill rate fell 7.3% while billable hours rose 7.2% - efficiency being competed into price, in reported numbers. And Unisys concedes in an audited 10-K that AI 'have reduced and replaced some of our historical services and solutions and will continue to do so'.

STAFFING IS BEING TAKEN PRIVATE, NOT RE-RATED. Three of four staffing names checked are gone: Guild delisted (Bayview, closed 2025-11-28), Heidrick & Struggles delisted (Advent + Corvex, closed 2025-12-10), Paycor delisted (Paychex, closed 2025-04-14). The fourth only LOOKS gone - ASGN renamed to Everforth (EFOR) effective 2026-04-24 with no Form 25 or 15 ever filed. Sponsors are buying the disruption-side cash flows at private marks while public multiples compress.

REGULATION IS A LARGER RETENTION KILLER THAN COMPETITION IN INSURANCE. OSCR and CLOV sit under statutory MLR floors (80/85%) that mechanically push admin savings back to members; TRUP's ~71% payout model commits the same by design; LMND and ROOT both state they route the saving into price to win share. Of the genuine adopters in insurance, almost none is positioned to keep the gain as margin - which is the parent record's D3 doubt, confirmed independently down-cap.

ANTI-MASKING / KEYWORD-SCREEN TRAPS WORTH KEEPING: MarketAxess has the highest AI keyword density in the market-infrastructure cohort and zero internal cost content. ManpowerGroup has the biggest savings headline ($200M by 2028) and it is ordinary restructuring, not AI. CBIZ's '$1 billion AI investment' headline belongs to Grant Thornton, its acquirer, not to CBIZ. A keyword screen picks up all three as adopters.

A CLEAN WITHIN-SECTOR CONTROL EXISTS. CorVel and Crawford & Company are both claims TPAs. CorVel's personnel/revenue fell 50.98% -> 47.67% over 8 audited quarters; Crawford's SG&A/revenue ROSE 22.11% -> 23.79% with operating margin flat at 2-4%. The sector is not producing this - one operator is. That is what makes CRVL a candidate rather than a sector call.

THE VENUE-AUTHORITY GRADIENT IS THE SINGLE BEST DISCRIMINATOR IN THIS SCREEN. AI cost claims cluster in CEO quotes and 8-K letters - PRAA 'global AI initiatives', ONIT 'AI-powered technologies', TBRG's targeted AI initiative, EVH's unnumbered 'AI targets', HSTM's 'AI transformation' executive appointment - and evaporate in 10-K and 10-Q MD&A. Only NNI (AI named as a contributor inside an audited cost bridge) and PHR (an executed headcount action) survive into a stronger venue. Grade venue before grading content.

THE ACTUAL COST LEVER IN LABOUR-HEAVY FINANCIAL SERVICES IN 2024-26 IS OFFSHORE PLUS SITE CONSOLIDATION, NOT AI - PRAA, TBRG, Encore's legacy Gurgaon and San Jose build, Onity's APAC operations. And it is aging: PRAA has largely finished its move and TBRG already concedes Indian wage inflation. An AI screen run over this cohort without an offshore control will mislabel labour arbitrage as automation.

RETENTION NOW HAS A FILED COUNTEREXAMPLE, WHICH THE PARENT RECORD LACKED. The parent's central unproven premise was whether adopters KEEP the gain. Nelnet's FY25 10-K shows a servicing cost-out explicitly 'partially offset by lower blended revenue per borrower under the new government servicing contract' - the saving repriced away by a monopsony buyer at renewal. Onity shows the softer version: its cost-to-service assumption fell $133 to $124 per loan, i.e. the improvement is already inside the MSR mark. Concentrated-buyer and contract-repriced structures are where retention demonstrably fails.

THE SPEND PHASE IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM THE ADOPTER PHASE ON A KEYWORD SCREEN AND OPPOSITE ON THE COST LINE. Onity books its RPA/ML/AI basket as technology expense rising .2M/+21% with no disclosed saving - the same shape the parent record caught at UWMC (six named AI products, only filed AI dollar a G&A increase). Two independent instances make it an archetype: require the cost line to move before crediting a named program, in either direction.

hiring_velocity_feasibility.signal_direction_inverted: For a plant ramp the tell is a posting WAVE. For an AI adopter the tell is the OPPOSITE - a sustained TAPER in ops-role postings while revenue grows. Read as attrition-without-backfill.

ranked.name: CorVel Corporation
ranked.case: CorVel is the textbook FAF filing signature reproduced down-cap, and it comes with its own within-sector control. Personnel expense over revenue fell 50.98% to 47.67% across the last 8 audited quarters, and the annual audited figures confirm it independently - 51.10% (FY24) to 49.77% (FY25) to 48.05% (FY26), with FY26 labor expense up just 3.3% against revenue up 7.0%. Operating margin moved 13.24% to 15.98% over the same window. This is a workers' compensation claims TPA and bill-review business where ops personnel ARE the cost to serve, so the ratio is measuring the right thing. Management has put internal-ops language into a filed document - the Q3-FY26 8-K states 'AI initiatives advanced materially across the organization... AI is augmenting operations by improving efficiency, shifting team capacity away from lower-value activities', and the safe-harbor legend formally lists 'improved productivity resulting from automation and augmentation across enterprise business systems' - though no number is attached anywhere. The reason this is a candidate rather than a sector call is Crawford & Company: same sector, same period, SG&A ratio RISING 22.11% to 23.79% with operating margin flat at 2-4%. The sector is not producing this; one operator is. The stock is down 32% over 52 weeks at the 31st percentile of its range, so the market is not paying for it. The honest weakness is retention: cost-containment services are frequently priced as a share of the savings delivered, which by contract design routes AI-driven savings to the customer and reprices them at renewal - and CorVel is partly a seller of AI bill review, so if carriers and TPAs bring that in-house the reason to outsource shrinks.
court_questions: Retention, the decisive question: quantify what share of revenue is share-of-savings or percentage-of-savings priced versus flat-fee or per-claim priced. If the majority is share-of-savings, the mechanism routes the gain to customers by contract and the whole case fails.

Attribution: separate genuine labor leverage from mix. Test the personnel ratio against claim volume and against case-mix - is CorVel handling more claims per employee, or handling a richer mix at the same productivity?
The disruption tail: CorVel sells AI bill review to payers. Model the scenario where its own customers deploy equivalent capability in-house and size the revenue-base erosion against the cost saving.
ranked.hiring_velocity: RUNNABLE AND HIGH-VALUE - verified live this run, 179 US postings with dates back to 2026-02-24, enough depth for a real taper read. Watch claims-examiner, adjuster and bill-review role counts specifically.

ranked.name: Paycom Software
ranked.case: Paycom has the single most unambiguous filed cost datum anywhere in this screen, and the stock is down 29%. The FY2025 10-K states in MD&A that 'automating our core business systems is creating new efficiencies that have led to reductions in headcount and, as a result, contributed to a decrease in certain employee-related expenses' - and the same filing supplies the numbers: headcount 7,306 at 12/31/24 to 5,770 at 12/31/25, down 1,536 people or 21.0% in one year, against revenue up 9.0% to $2,051.7M, with cost of revenue falling from 17.8% to 16.8% of revenue. The Q1-2026 10-Q carries it forward with a forward-looking claim, which is rare in a filed document. Retention on the cost saving is genuinely strong - mid-market payroll is a three-to-four-player oligopoly with system-of-record switching costs, year-end tax continuity and painful re-implementation - and so far the saving has stayed as margin rather than being priced away. The tension, which Paycom discloses against itself, is that the exact same automation wave cuts the other way on revenue: Paycom is priced per employee, and its own risk factor warns that AI 'may reduce our clients' need for existing or future employees who are or would be potential users of our solution'. That is why this name belongs in a court rather than on a buy list - the adopter benefit is booked and visible now, the disruption risk is on the revenue line later, and the market appears to be pricing the second over the first. Our XBRL series is consistent with that reading: despite the 21% headcount cut, consolidated operating margin moved only +0.44pp, so the saving is currently being spent rather than dropped.
court_questions: The central bear: quantify the per-employee-priced revenue base's sensitivity to client headcount. What client-employee attrition rate offsets the entire cost saving, and what is observable in reported clients and employees-on-platform today?

Where did the money go: headcount fell 21% and consolidated operating margin moved only +0.44pp. Bridge the gap - reinvestment, pricing concession, mix, or stock comp - because the answer decides whether this is operating leverage or a cost-out being spent.
Is a 21% one-year headcount cut repeatable or a one-time reset? Grade the FY2026 headcount disclosure as the falsifier.
ranked.hiring_velocity: RUNNABLE - single dominant Oklahoma City campus plus named service centers makes the site read unusually clean. A continued posting taper in service and R&D roles corroborates; a re-acceleration falsifies.

ranked.name: Alight Inc - Class A
ranked.case: Alight is the best D2 conjunction in the entire small/mid screen - the only name with a board-approved named program that explicitly names AI as the lever, a quantified savings figure, and that figure disclosed in a 10-Q rather than a deck. The 10-K describes the Post-Separation Plan as including 'simplifying our post-divestiture operating model, rationalizing our technology spend, expanding our use of artificial intelligence and automation and continued optimization of real estate', and the 10-Q states the company 'estimates an annual savings of over $75 million after the PSP is completed' against roughly $65M of pre-tax restructuring cost over a 15-month period from Q2 2025. Against a market cap of $795M, $75M of annual savings is not a rounding error - it is the whole equity story if it lands. The pricing structure is the second reason it ranks: revenue is a contracted fee per participant per period on three-to-five-year terms, so efficiency does not mechanically reduce billings the way per-FTE BPO pricing does, and the gain reaches margin inside the term with giveback risk deferred to renewal. That is the single best retention structure found in the BPO cohort. Everything else about this name is broken, which is why it is fourth and not first: the reported operating margin series is dominated by goodwill impairment and is unusable as a signal, the price has collapsed from a 52-week high of $100.68 to $16.98 on a separation and share-count change that makes the price history non-comparable without careful adjustment, and the balance sheet carries leverage into a program that is a promise rather than a result. This is a high-variance, evidence-rich, execution-dependent candidate, not a quality compounder.
court_questions: Split the $75M, which is now the first question rather than an assumption: AI and automation is one of FOUR named levers alongside operating-model simplification, technology-spend rationalization and real-estate optimization, with no split disclosed. And the PSP severance booked to date is only about $21M ($20M FY2025 + $1M Q1-2026), which is too small to generate $75M of headcount savings - so quantify how much of the program is labor at all.

Cap structure and price-history reconstruction BEFORE any valuation statement: reconcile the separation, any share-count change and the debt schedule. The parent doctrine requires cap structure before any EV or net-cash claim, and this name's broken price history is exactly where that gets fumbled.

Delivery evidence and solvency runway: SG&A/revenue is already down 3.96pp over 8 quarters - specify the dated bar that separates PSP-as-AI-leverage from PSP-as-ordinary-restructuring, grade it against the predecessor Transformation Program which spent $140M, and confirm the balance sheet survives a 15-month program.
ranked.hiring_velocity: RUNNABLE but THIN - verified live, 75 US postings back to 2026-05-21. Enough for a coarse trend, not for a sharp taper read; treat as corroborating only.

ranked.name: Maximus Inc
ranked.case: Maximus is the most labor-intensive name of any scale in the screen - 37,200 employees against $146k of revenue per employee - running government eligibility, assessment and appeals processing, which is exactly the case-handling work that converts to software, and it trades at the 16th percentile of its 52-week range. The retention structure is the best in the slate and it is structural rather than hopeful: the majority of the US Federal Services book is transaction- and outcome-priced - paid per assessment or appeal processed, per participant - not per FTE, so handling a case with less labor drops to margin inside the contract term, with giveback deferred to slow government re-procurement. But this name was demoted from rank 1 on verification, and the correction matters. The filed attribution is weaker than it first appeared: the FY2025 10-K says 'Our margins received a benefit from the implementation of technology initiatives, which increased the productivity of our operations' - technology initiatives, not AI - and it is the fifth item in a list whose other members are clinical and medical-assessment volume growth, FEMA disaster-response revenue that the filing itself calls unpredictable in extent and timing, Honoring our PACT Act volumes plus a scale-expanding contract rebid, and a reduced share of performance penalties. The margin step itself, 12.2% to 15.3%, already happened in FY2025, and management guides FY2026 to only 15.5-16.0% - a further +0.2 to +0.7pp that is priced by definition. Our consolidated XBRL series is consistent with a segment story that has not become a company story: operating margin +1.79pp with the SG&A ratio flat. Maximus stays on the slate because the labor intensity and the outcome-priced contract structure are both genuinely rare, but it enters as a name where the AI content is asserted by inference, not by the filing.
court_questions: Separate technology from volume and from FEMA: build the FY24->FY25 segment margin bridge across all five named drivers and show what the technology line is actually worth in basis points. If it is not separable, the AI thesis has no measurable object here.

D6 dominance: the step is US Federal Services only while consolidated margin moved 1.79pp on a flat SG&A ratio. Decompose consolidated margin by segment and state whether the automation leg can ever dominate the print.

D4: FY2026 segment margin is GUIDED at 15.5-16.0%. Guided margin is priced by definition - the ADP problem. Establish what would have to beat the guide, and separately whether the 17% 52-week-range percentile is federal budget and re-procurement risk rather than mispricing.
ranked.hiring_velocity: RUNNABLE - large, named, US-concentrated ops sites; ops-role vocabulary variant needed. High value here because government program staffing is site-identifiable.

ranked.name: HealthEquity
ranked.case: HealthEquity surfaced only after the cost-of-revenue blind spot was closed, and it then produced the largest cost-ratio decline in the re-test: cost of revenue fell 34.49% to 29.34% of revenue over 8 audited quarters, a 5.15pp move that the SG&A-based screen had scored as flat. The FY26 10-K supplies the dollar figure and the attribution in MD&A - 'Service costs $328.5M vs $351.6M, a decrease of $23.1M or 7%... primarily due to efficiencies resulting from our technology investments and a decrease in costs incurred to reimburse members impacted by outside fraud activity' - achieved while total accounts GREW, which is the operating-leverage shape this thesis is looking for. The AI language is stated as an internal cost objective in both Item 1 and MD&A: 'we also increasingly use AI tools and technologies to improve customer service, lower costs, and increase efficiencies' and 'We utilize AI to streamline administrative processes.' Member support is a genuine ops-personnel cost base with a seasonal support-centre ramp, so the mechanism has a real object. Retention is good but NOT the clean structural pass this screen first credited it with - a correction worth carrying. HSA administration is priced per account through sticky employer and health-plan channels with custodial economics attached, so a service-cost saving is not clawed back the way an RCM or government-servicing contract reprices it. But the fuller filing read finds secular per-account service-fee compression in HSA administration, so a meaningful part of the saving should be expected to be competed into Network Partner pricing at renewal. Grade retention MODERATE-TO-GOOD, not best-in-screen. Two real offsets keep it at rank 5 rather than higher. AI is not separately credited - management says 'technology investments', and part of the $23.1M is fraud-reimbursement normalisation rather than efficiency. And the dominant driver of the roughly 9pp operating-margin gain is custodial yield, which is rate-driven, so the D6 dominance test has an unfavourable answer: a rate cut hurts the margin story far more than automation helps it.
court_questions: D6 dominance and the rate denominator: decompose the ~9pp operating-margin gain into custodial yield, service-cost decline and opex leverage. If custodial yield dominates, this is a rates stock with an efficiency side story - and the parent record's JPM lesson is exactly that a rate-driven line manufactures a fake efficiency read.

Split the $23.1M: how much is technology efficiency versus fraud-reimbursement normalisation, which is a one-time normalisation and not a slope? Management guides FY27 service costs 'relatively steady' as efficiencies offset account growth - that guide is the testable bar.

Retention, now the sharpened question after the grade was walked back from best-in-screen to moderate-to-good: has revenue per account fallen over the same window that service costs fell? If per-account fees are compressing at a similar rate, the saving is already being competed into Network Partner pricing and the structural argument fails.

D4 entry, added after the live quote: HQY is at the 84th percentile of its 52-week range at $100.61 and up 5.9% y/y - closer to the done-and-paid shape than the rest of the slate. Establish whether the market is already paying for the service-cost slope or only for custodial yield.
ranked.hiring_velocity: RUNNABLE - member-support centres are named and geographically concentrated; support-representative posting counts against account growth is close to a direct read of the thesis.
ranked.retention_proxy_correction: FIRST DRAFT OVER-CLAIMED. Initially graded best-in-screen and structural. Corrected to moderate-to-good: network-partner integrations and HSA custody are real switching costs, but HSA administration carries secular per-account fee compression, so part of any service-cost saving gets competed into Network Partner pricing at renewal. Recording the walk-back because over-crediting retention is the parent record's specific known failure mode - D3 is its central UNPROVEN premise and this screen should not quietly resolve it in a candidate's favour.

ranked.name: Cass Information Systems
ranked.case: Cass is the purest ops-personnel business in the screen and the clearest instance of the parent record's most useful pattern - real cost-out that is never called AI, and is therefore unpriced by construction. It processes freight and utility invoices: the cost base is literally data entry, exception handling and audit labor, which is the workload large language models and modern OCR attack most directly. Personnel expense over revenue fell 61.45% to 55.56% across 8 audited quarters, a 5.89pp decline on a business where labor is roughly 60% of revenue, and operating margin moved from 11.93% to 22.16%. The company says nothing at all: the sole AI mention in the entire 10-K is a risk factor about deficient AI. That silence is the thesis - it is the FIS archetype from the large-cap pass, where genuine headcount reduction gets labeled 'reorganization' and no AI premium is ever paid. Retention is structurally decent: invoice processing is sticky and bank-adjacent with real switching cost, plus float income on the payment balances. Two caveats are serious enough that this ranks fifth rather than second. First, Cass is a bank holding company, so the 'Revenues' denominator includes net interest income that moved with the rate cycle - the parent record's JPM lesson is precisely that a rate-driven revenue denominator manufactures a fake efficiency-ratio improvement, and that contamination must be stripped before the 5.89pp is believed. Second, at $55.92 the stock is at the 96th percentile of its 52-week range and up 44%, which is the 'done and paid' shape.
court_questions: Strip the denominator, which is the whole verification: recompute personnel expense against FEE revenue only, excluding net interest income, across the same 8 quarters. If the 5.89pp decline survives, the finding is real; if it collapses, this is the JPM rate-denominator artifact and the name is dead.
Volume normalisation: get invoices and transactions processed per employee. A falling labor ratio on falling volume is cost-cutting; on rising volume it is leverage.
D4: at the 96th percentile and +44%, establish what the market thinks it is paying for - rate-driven net interest income or the processing margin - because those re-rate very differently from here.
ranked.hiring_velocity: RUNNABLE - concentrated St Louis and Columbus operations centers. Processing and audit-clerk role counts are the exact substitution surface; a taper here is a clean corroborant.

ranked.name: Phreesia
ranked.case: Phreesia carries the only AI-attributed headcount ACTION found anywhere in this screen - not an intention, not a program description, an executed reduction. The 10-K states the company sees 'significant opportunities to reduce our reliance on manual processes across Phreesia through the adoption of artificial intelligence', and that was executed as the May 2026 restructuring: the 10-Q records approximately 220 positions eliminated, and the accompanying 8-K EX-99.2 stakeholder letter supplies the attribution - roughly 100 internal engineering and product roles plus roughly 100 contractors, which 'reflects how AI is changing the way we build and deploy software.' Management then held FY27 adjusted EBITDA guidance at $125-135M despite cutting the revenue outlook by roughly $35-39M, which is the clearest available statement that the cost action is expected to hold. Our audited series is consistent: operating margin improved 10.55pp over 8 quarters to roughly break-even with the SG&A ratio down. Retention is favourable in structure - Phreesia is priced on per-client subscriptions, so removing internal labour does not shrink the billing base the way per-FTE or per-hour pricing does. Three things hold it at rank 7. The attribution fuses two documents - the number is in the 10-Q and the AI reason is in an 8-K letter, and citing 'Phreesia cut 220 jobs because of AI' as a single filed fact would be exactly the venue error this screen is built to catch. The cuts are engineering and contractor roles, which is AI changing how software gets built rather than AI removing cost-to-serve, so it is adjacent to the thesis rather than central to it. And Phreesia is substantially a SELLER of patient-intake automation with a decelerating top line, so it is currently spending the saving to defend guidance rather than dropping it to margin.
court_questions: Is this cost-to-serve or R&D? The cuts were roughly 100 engineering and product roles plus 100 contractors, not service or support staff. Establish whether Phreesia's actual ops cost-to-serve line is moving at all, because only that version supports this thesis.

Guidance arithmetic: adjusted EBITDA held at $125-135M while revenue guidance was cut $35-39M. Verify the bridge and determine whether the cost action is being consumed by revenue deceleration - i.e. margin defence, not margin expansion.
The seller-side tail: Phreesia self-discloses AI demand risk. Size the scenario where customers' own AI reduces the need for third-party intake automation against the internal saving.

D4 entry, added after the live quote: PHR is at the 12th percentile of its 52-week range at $10.73 and down 59% y/y. That is a decelerating-revenue de-rate, not a mispriced cost story - confirm the cost action is not simply being consumed by the top-line decline before treating the cheapness as opportunity.
ranked.hiring_velocity: RUNNABLE and unusually well-suited - a software and services firm with heavy remote posting volume; an engineering-role posting freeze following the May-2026 action is directly observable and would confirm the cut is structural rather than a hiring pause.

ranked.name: Stewart Information Services
ranked.case: Stewart is carried as a RE-RANK ON NEW EVIDENCE, not as a new name - the house has it at WATCH 5/10 from the 2026-07-29 pair ruling, and nothing here reopens that. What this pass adds is that Stewart has the best filed INTENT language in the entire screen after Lemonade, stated in both the 10-K and the 10-Q: 'Our plans to improve margins include additional automation of manual processes, further consolidation of our various systems and production operations', and specifically AI deployed 'to automate and streamline certain manual processes during title search, insurance policy issuance and real estate transaction settlement... increase efficiency, reduce costs'. Title search, exam and curative work is precisely the document labor AI eats, and the personnel ratio has moved the right way - 29.84% to 28.30% over 8 audited quarters. The retention argument here is the strongest in insurance and comes straight from the house's own FAF pair court: title rates are filed and regulated in many states, so the price leg is sticky inside the rate cycle and a cost saving is not immediately competed away - the regulatory inversion that makes title the one place the parent record found retention partially printing. What holds it at rank seven is that there is no number attached to any of the intent language, the earlier Q2 agency-mix masking finding still stands on its own window and means Stewart's headline ratios need care, the FHFA title-waiver policy axis is shared with FAF and FNF so this is not an independent bet, and volume in the rate cycle swamps the AI delta in any single quarter.
court_questions: Does this beat the resting expression? The house already assigned the title slot to FAF and holds a FNF-from-48 resting order. Establish whether STC adds anything beyond a third vehicle on one policy bet - the pair-court precedent applies and the default answer should be no.

The masking check must be repeated: separate the netted ratio from the labor-bearing title-segment ratio, since the Q2 headline improvement was previously shown to be agency-mix denominator inflation.
Freeze the falsifier: what does the personnel ratio need to print, on which date, for the automation claim to survive - and is that bar distinguishable from ordinary title-volume operating leverage?
ranked.hiring_velocity: RUNNABLE - large branch and title-plant footprint. Title examiner, searcher and escrow-assistant postings are the substitution surface; a taper against rising order counts would be the corroborant.
